sentences.text: Revenue, net interest income plus noninterest income, rose from $96.6 billion in FY2016 to $182 billion in FY2025, a 7.3% CAGR [D5][D206].
The path was a step change rather than a smooth compound: revenue was $121.6 billion in FY2021 and $158 billion in FY2023, a 30% jump in two years [D110][D159].
Net interest income rose 33.8% in FY2023 to $89.3 billion, with interest income at $171 billion [D174][F8][X125].
FY2025 growth slowed to 2.8%, with net interest income up 3.1% and noninterest income up 2.4% [D226][D221][D222].
North America supplied the bulk of growth, contributing 20.6pp of the FY2023 revenue increase and 10.2pp in FY2024, before fading to 0.2pp in FY2025 [D245][D248][D251].
Asia-Pacific was the fastest-growing geography in FY2025, up 17.3% and contributing 1.2pp, with EMEA adding 1.2pp on 9.5% growth [D300][D301][D275][D276].

The FY2025 net interest income increase came from higher Markets net interest income, higher Card Services revolving balances and higher wholesale deposit balances, largely offset by deposit margin compression [P28].
Operating costs grew 1.4pp faster than revenue in FY2025, at 4.2% against 2.8% [D225][D226].
EPS grew faster than net income over the window, 13.9% against 9.7% CAGR, as the diluted share count fell 3.4% in FY2025 alone [F115][F113][D224].
The efficiency ratio was 52.4% in FY2025, against a 57.2% window median and a 51.7% window low in FY2024 [D207][D333][D331].
That is the best cost discipline in the peer group, at the 0th percentile against a 61.7% median for seven banks [D336][D337].

Noninterest expense rose 4% to $95.6 billion on higher compensation, brokerage and distribution fees, auto lease depreciation and technology and marketing spend, partly offset by FDIC special assessment releases [P26][X137].
In FY2025 net margin of 31.2% sat 21.2pp below the 52.3% net interest income share of revenue, with the 7.8% credit-loss provision and 52.4% efficiency ratio the gap [D210][D209][D208][D207].
Operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure for a bank; it swung to -$147.8 billion in FY2025 from -$42.0 billion in FY2024 [F60][F59].
The FY2025 outflow came from higher trading assets, higher securities borrowed, net loan originations and higher other assets, partly offset by net income and higher trading liabilities [P21].
Capital return is the better test: buybacks plus dividends of $48.2 billion were 85% of the $57.0 billion net income [D205][F30].
Return on average equity was 16.1% in FY2025, at the 100th percentile against an 11.8% peer median [D213][D338][D339].
Shareholders' equity reached $362 billion against $4.42 trillion of assets, with loans of $1.47 trillion at 57.3% of $2.56 trillion of deposits [F110][F90][X197][X207][D211].
Loans grew $121.1 billion, driven by CIB Markets and AWM securities-based lending on higher client demand [P4].
FY2025 buybacks of $31.6 billion and dividends of $16.6 billion exceeded the prior year's $33.6 billion combined, and the diluted share count fell 3.4% [X102][X112][D182][D224].
The credit-loss provision rose to 7.8% of revenue in FY2025 from 6.0% in FY2024, above the 6.0% peer median and at the 75th percentile of four banks [D208][D185][D341][D340].
Criticized wholesale exposure of $48.5 billion, up from $44.7 billion, and rising nonaccruals point to a credit cycle turning rather than a one-quarter charge [P2][P1].
Net income for FY2021 to FY2025 in the table comes from the proxy pay-versus-performance table, not the 10-K, and differs by up to 0.10% [R1][F26][X16][F30][X20].
The gap is immaterial to the trend but the 10-K figures should be used where precision matters [R1].
Whether the efficiency ratio holds below the 57.2% window median or drifts back toward the 59.2% FY2022 high, reported in the FY2026 10-K [D333][D332].
Whether the credit-loss provision stays above the 6.0% peer median or falls back toward the 5.0% FY2022 level, in the FY2026 10-K [D341][D136].
Whether net interest income growth recovers from 3.1% toward the 12.3% three-year revenue CAGR, in the FY2026 10-K [D221][D335].
